Divergence controls entropy in distillation

Nicolas Zucchet    Scott W. Linderman Affiliation: Stanford University Email: {nzucchet,slinderman}@stanford.edu
Abstract

Distillation has become a core primitive of large language model training, but its properties are not yet well understood. We take an entropic perspective, studying how the entropy of the student depends on the data and the divergence that define the distillation objective. We prove that forward KL inflates the entropy of the student above that of the teacher. Since cross-entropy training is a special case, this yields an identity that we verify quantitatively in pretraining and supervised finetuning. Other divergences come with no such guarantee: reverse KL deflates entropy until the gap between student and teacher gets too large, and interpolating between the two changes entropy smoothly early in training but abruptly at convergence. The lower entropy of on-policy distillation comes from token-level reverse KL, not from on-policy sampling. The divergence therefore acts as an implicit entropy regularizer, whose role is clearest in self-distillation: as conditioning on privileged information deflates entropy, the divergence hyperparameters that work best are those that compensate for it.

1 Introduction

Distillation consists of training a student model to mimic the behavior of a teacher model and compress its knowledge (Hinton et al., 2015). It is used in increasingly diverse contexts for large language models, from pretraining lightweight, more efficient models (Muralidharan et al., 2024; Gemma Team, 2025), to solidifying reasoning abilities in posttraining (Ma et al., 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2026). In practice, distillation amounts to minimizing a divergence between two categorical probability distributions. While divergence minimization has been extensively studied elsewhere (Minka, 2005; Bishop, 2006; Amari, 2016), its properties are not yet well understood in the context of large language models.

In this work, we study the properties of these algorithms from an entropic perspective, investigating how design choices affect the entropy of the student. Entropy is fundamentally a measure of uncertainty, whether in thermodynamics (Boltzmann, 1877) or information theory (Shannon, 1948), and it is particularly important for large language models as it relates to the diversity of the output distribution (Kirk et al., 2024; Farquhar et al., 2024) and controls exploration in reinforcement learning (Cui et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025). It is also easy to compute and log during any training run. Here, we develop intuition for how distillation shapes entropy.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • –

    Decoupling sampling and divergence choice (Section 2). We review distillation, decoupling the choice of the data generation process from that of the divergence, which enables us to study their effects on the student’s entropy independently.

  • –

    From divergence to entropy (Section 3). In a toy model of language modeling, we show that: forward KL inflates the student’s entropy above the teacher’s by the residual divergence; reverse KL deflates it until mimicking the teacher gets too difficult and then suddenly inflates it; and interpolating between the two varies entropy smoothly early in training but abruptly at convergence. Top-kk restrictions also shift entropy, depending on how the tail is handled.

  • –

    At scale, the divergence implicitly controls entropy (Section 4). After pretraining and supervised finetuning, the entropy of a language model matches the cross-entropy loss it was trained to minimize; larger models therefore have lower entropy. When distilling from a larger teacher, the divergence drives entropy more than on- vs. off-policy sampling; in self-distillation, it counters the entropy drop that conditioning on privileged information induces.

2 Decoupling sampling and divergence choice in distillation

Distillation algorithms, in particular on-policy ones, are often derived by minimizing a divergence between the student’s and the teacher’s distributions over sequences of tokens. As we will argue, this couples the choice of token-level objective with the sampling distribution, which makes their respective effects on the student hard to disentangle and can yield suboptimal configurations. Following Czarnecki et al. (2019) and Agarwal et al. (2024) inter alia, we decouple the two, as summarized in Figure 1 and detailed in Appendix A.

Student, teacher and sampling distributions.

We consider data consisting of prompts xx and completions yy generated by a sampling distribution pp. On these completions, the student distribution πθ​(y∣x)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x) parametrized by θ\theta is compared to that of the teacher π∗​(y∣x)\pi^{*}(y\mid x). The sampling distribution pp can either be the student itself, in which case learning is on-policy, or the teacher, in which case we call it off-policy distillation. The teacher can either be explicit or implicit, as when training on internet text through next-token cross-entropy minimization.

Distillation objective.

The objective of distillation is to minimize the expected divergence between the student and the teacher over a dataset of prompts xx and completions yy,

ℒ(θ)=𝔼x𝔼y∼p(⋅∣x)[∑t=1Tℓ(πθ(⋅∣x,y<t),π∗(⋅∣x,y<t))],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right]\!, (1)

with TT the length of the completion and ℓ\ell a divergence between the full next-token distributions of the two models, such as the forward or the reverse KL. The objective is here defined at the token level, which is what enables us to decouple the sampling distribution pp from the divergence choice ℓ\ell. Otherwise, the sampling distribution would be implicitly defined by the divergence choice—a sequence-level reverse KL forces on-policy data and a sequence-level forward KL forces off-policy data. In practice, gradients are typically not backpropagated through the sampling process, even when it is the student itself, with rare exceptions (Gu et al., 2024, e.g.,). The same approximation is used when improving the reasoning abilities of language models through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Lambert et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025). It amounts to ignoring the score function term, which biases the gradient but considerably reduces its variance (Williams, 1992; Roeder et al., 2017; Naesseth et al., 2018; Fu et al., 2026). This observation motivates ignoring sequence modeling aspects of distillation in our toy model of Section 3.1.

Entropy.

Core to our analysis is the average entropy of the model π\pi, which we define as

H¯(π)=𝔼x𝔼y∼p(⋅∣x)[1T∑t=1TH(π(⋅∣x,y<t))],\bar{H}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}H\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right]\!, (2)

with HH the Shannon entropy of a distribution over the vocabulary. The distribution π\pi need not be the one that generates the contexts (x,y<t)(x,y_{<t}). When p=π=πθp=\pi=\pi_{\theta}, this is the student’s normalized sequence-level entropy.

3 Properties of divergences and their effect on entropy

The formalism of the previous section enables us to study the effect of the sampling distribution and the divergence choice independently. In this section, we restrict ourselves to that of the divergence as it is more tractable to analyze theoretically, and defer the empirical study of the sampling distribution to the next section. We first introduce a toy model that captures part of language modeling and use it as an illustrative example to highlight the properties of different divergence functions.

3.1 A toy model of language modeling

The canonical example to illustrate the properties of forward and reverse KL divergences is fitting a mixture of Gaussians with a single Gaussian distribution (Bishop, 2006). While this has been used to illustrate some of the properties of distillation or reinforcement learning in the context of large language models (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026; Nicolicioiu et al., 2026), its continuous and non-neural-network nature makes it an imperfect proxy for what happens in practice.

Instead, we propose the following toy model, which takes as input a random embedding eie_{i} associated with each context ii in the data distribution and outputs a next-token distribution through

πθ(⋅∣i)=softmax(Wei).\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)=\mathrm{softmax}(We_{i}). (3)

Such a model can be understood as the prediction head of a language model whose preceding sequence model provides random embeddings, as an associative memory model (Cabannes et al., 2024; Nichani et al., 2025; Zucchet et al., 2025), or as the simplest neural network that can produce categorical distributions over possible next tokens. This model has been shown to be able to fit a number of contexts proportional to the number of parameters of the linear layer (Cabannes et al., 2024; Nichani et al., 2025). Varying the number of contexts therefore allows us to control the difficulty of the task, or equivalently the capacity of an implicit teacher. Another knob is the entropy of the teacher distribution, or equivalently the teacher perplexity exp⁡(H⁡(π∗))\exp(H(\pi^{*})), that is the effective number of tokens over which the teacher places probability mass; increasing it also makes the task harder (Zucchet et al., 2026).

Contrary to language models, this toy model has no sequence modeling component, which makes it easier to analyze theoretically. Little is lost since gradients are not propagated through the sampling process: in both cases, the distillation objective mostly aims at improving next-token prediction and not at shaping the sequence sampling distribution directly.

Throughout this section, we leverage this model when needed to illustrate some of the theoretical properties of the different divergences. In our simulations, as a default we set the embedding dimension to 128128, the vocabulary size to 6464, the number of contexts to 20482048, and sample the teacher perplexity log-uniformly between 11 and 1616. The model is trained with full-batch Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) and a learning rate of 0.10.1 for 4040k steps; Appendix B.7 details the setup.

3.2 Divergence choice only matters when student and teacher differ

Before characterizing what each divergence does to entropy, it is worth delimiting when the choice matters at all. Indeed, a well-established property of KL divergences is that the geometries of the forward and the reverse KL are equivalent around optimality (Amari, 2016). In our case, this means that if the student is capable of reproducing the teacher and already starts close to it, the learning dynamics of distillation with forward and reverse KL are the same. Both objectives also share the same global optimum πθ=π∗\pi_{\theta}=\pi^{*}. More formally, when πθ\pi_{\theta} is close to π∗\pi^{*} on all contexts ii, we have

∇θ𝔼i[DKL(π∗(⋅∣i)∥πθ(⋅∣i))]≈∇θ𝔼i[DKL(πθ(⋅∣i)∥π∗(⋅∣i))]\nabla_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i))\right]\approx\nabla_{\theta}\,\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i))\right] (4)

up to first order. The student’s entropy is therefore also the same along the training trajectory under either objective. We emphasize that the statement is independent of the sampling distribution pp, as long as it stays constant during training. This argument applies more broadly to any ff-divergence, and in particular to the generalized Jensen–Shannon family that we use later. A proof of the general statement can be found in Appendix B.1.

A consequence of that result is that any difference in behavior induced by the choice of divergence occurs when the student and the teacher distributions differ significantly, e.g., because the student cannot represent the teacher or because the two start far from each other. The rest of this section will implicitly assume that we are in such a regime. Figure 2b illustrates part of this property in our toy model: for a small enough number of contexts, the student and the teacher have almost identical entropy at convergence regardless of the divergence choice, as the student is close to matching the teacher.

3.3 Forward KL predictably inflates entropy

The forward KL divergence is known to be mode-covering (Bishop, 2006; Murphy, 2022): as

DKL(π∗(⋅∣i)∥πθ(⋅∣i))=∑jπ∗(j∣i)logπ∗​(j∣i)πθ​(j∣i)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i))=\sum_{j}\pi^{*}(j\mid i)\log\frac{\pi^{*}(j\mid i)}{\pi_{\theta}(j\mid i)} (5)

the objective diverges whenever π∗​(j∣i)>0\pi^{*}(j\mid i)>0 and πθ​(j∣i)→0\pi_{\theta}(j\mid i)\rightarrow 0, so the student tends to cover all of the teacher’s support. From this intuition, we expect the student to have higher entropy than the teacher; we now show that this does indeed hold at optimality.

Take a neural network with a linear softmax head. This includes standard language model heads as well as our toy model of Section 3.1. At optimality, if we were to multiply the weight matrix by a scalar factor, the loss would not change up to first order. The consequence of that, which we prove in Appendix B.3 following classical arguments from information geometry (Amari, 2016), is that

H¯(πθfor∗)=H¯(π∗)+𝔼i[DKL(π∗(⋅∣i)∥πθfor∗(⋅∣i))]\bar{H}(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})=\bar{H}(\pi^{*})+\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}(\cdot\mid i))\right] (6)

when θfor∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}} is a local optimum of the forward KL distillation objective. In particular, the student necessarily has higher entropy than the teacher on average, which Figure 2b and 2c confirm. This statement is only relative to the teacher: the forward KL can still deflate entropy over the course of learning if the teacher’s entropy is much lower, as Figure 2e illustrates.

Given that the cross-entropy loss minimization objective can be seen as off-policy distillation with the forward KL, in which continuations of the data are samples from an implicit teacher, this result extends to pretraining and supervised finetuning as well. Expanding the KL, Equation 6 states that the average entropy of the student equals its average cross-entropy with the teacher, that is its training loss, both measured on the training data. This does not require the two distributions to be close. It only requires a softmax head, as in large language models, and a student at a stationary point of the average forward KL. A direct consequence is that, among models trained to convergence, a higher loss comes with a higher entropy: a student that cannot match its teacher ends up more uncertain rather than overconfident. The experiments of Section 4.1 will confirm that these statements hold quantitatively in practice.

3.4 Reverse KL deflates entropy until the gap gets too large

Whereas the forward KL is mode-covering, the reverse KL is mode-seeking (MacKay, 2003; Bishop, 2006; Margossian & Saul, 2023). This mode-seeking bias of the reverse KL divergence suggests that a student trained with it would have lower entropy than the teacher. In practice, this is indeed the case in a wide range of scenarios, but breaks when the task becomes too hard, as illustrated in Figure 2b and 2c when there are too many contexts to model or when the teacher is too diffuse.

Theoretical analysis is not as easy as for the forward KL, so we focus on providing intuition for why this happens.11 1 The stationarity argument behind Equation 6 also applies to the reverse KL, but it then constrains the spread of the log probabilities of the student rather than its entropy (Appendix B.4). Let us start by rewriting the reverse KL divergence as

DKL(πθ(⋅∣i)∥π∗(⋅∣i))=−∑jπθ(j∣i)logπ∗(j∣i)−H(πθ(⋅∣i)).D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i))=-\sum_{j}\pi_{\theta}(j\mid i)\log\pi^{*}(j\mid i)-H(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)). (7)

The first term is the mode-seeking part of the divergence: whenever π∗​(j∣i)→0\pi^{*}(j\mid i)\rightarrow 0, the student must place low probability mass on token jj to avoid a large loss. As the teacher gets more diffuse, the first term flattens out, and the second one, which pushes the student’s entropy up, dominates the objective. As a result, the mode-seeking bias of the reverse KL disappears and the student ends up inflating its entropy. We can formalize that intuition by analyzing the behavior of the reverse KL divergence in the limit of a flat teacher distribution. This analysis, provided in Appendix B.5, shows that the reverse KL divergence, as well as any divergence in the generalized Jensen–Shannon family, becomes equivalent to the forward KL divergence in that limit, and therefore inflates entropy. It does not predict the exact point at which the transition occurs, but it does quantify how the entropy gap between the teacher and the student evolves: the gap widens as the number of contexts grows and narrows as the teacher gets more diffuse, matching Figure 2b and 2c.

One may wonder whether the inflation part of the statement is relevant in practice: in the toy experiments it only occurs when the number of contexts is large or the teacher’s output diversity is high, cases in which distillation is unlikely to bring significant performance improvements. In our large language model experiments of Section 4, we do not observe any average entropy inflation with the reverse KL. That said, the analysis here still gives us some insight into the biases of the reverse KL divergence. Even when inflation does not hold on average, it should still occur on a subset of contexts, and the intuition developed here hints at which ones are more likely to see the entropy of their next-token distribution inflated.

3.5 In between forward and reverse KL, entropy can sharply change

Forward and reverse KL are not the only divergences used in practice, and it is common to interpolate between the two through the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence (von Werra et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2024; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b; Xing et al., 2026). We wonder whether the entropy of the student smoothly and monotonically increases as we interpolate between the two divergences. The results, illustrated in Figure 2d and 2e, show that it depends on the stage of training: early in training entropy smoothly decreases as the interpolation weight λ\lambda increases (Figure 2e), whereas at convergence it drops abruptly (Figure 2d). That said, the phase transition boundary does evolve smoothly as a function of λ\lambda, cf. Figure 7 in the appendix, and divergences with larger λ\lambda values need harder tasks to inflate entropy. As a result, one of the consequences of picking a divergence in the generalized Jensen–Shannon family is an implicit regularization on the entropy of the student, which can be either smooth or sharp depending on the training stage.

3.6 Top-kk restrictions shift entropy depending on how the tail is handled

An important design choice that we have not yet touched upon is how much of the total probability distribution to take into account when computing the divergence. So far, we have only used full vocabulary divergences, but in practice it is common to restrict the divergence to the top-kk tokens of the teacher or student distribution for compute and bandwidth efficiency (Fu et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2026). Two choices arise: which distribution selects the top-kk tokens (student or teacher), and how the mass outside the selected set is handled. The renormalized variant renormalizes both distributions over the top-kk tokens (Fu et al., 2026; Xing et al., 2026), whereas the tail bucket keeps the tail mass as one extra bucket (Hübotter et al., 2026; Huang & Wei, 2026); see Appendix A.2.2.

We find that top-kk restrictions can have a non-negligible effect on the entropy of the student and that the effect depends strongly on the two design choices above. When the student selects the top-kk tokens, renormalization keeps entropy relatively independent of kk, at least early on, whereas the tail bucket yields increasingly large entropies as kk decreases. When the teacher selects the top-kk tokens, the early-training picture reverses. The results presented here hold for the forward KL divergence, and we additionally sweep over the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence weight λ\lambda in Figure 8 in the appendix, finding that these observations are mostly independent of the choice of divergence, although we observe some interactions.

4 Entropy in different distillation scenarios

We now turn to empirical validation of the intuition and of the theoretical properties of divergences derived in the previous section, as well as to studying the effect of the sampling distribution. We consider three settings, which are both practically relevant and will enable us to test different parts of the theory: pretraining, distillation in posttraining for reasoning, and self-distillation.

4.1 Cross-entropy predicts entropy in pretraining and supervised finetuning

Next-token cross-entropy minimization as used during pretraining and supervised finetuning can be understood as sampled off-policy distillation with forward KL, in which the teacher is an implicit distribution over continuations of the data. In that case the divergence is fixed: we only have access to samples from the teacher distribution, so we cannot use reverse KL or any other divergence that would require direct access to the teacher’s probabilities. As discussed in Section 3.3, Equation 6 predicts that the entropy of the student is equal to its cross-entropy loss at convergence, both measured on the training data. Testing it requires the cross-entropy form of the statement, which only needs samples from the teacher, rather than its form in terms of the entropy of the teacher and the KL divergence to it, which needs the probabilities of the teacher. Yet, compute-optimal large language models are typically stopped before convergence (Kaplan et al., 2020), although the trend is to longer pretraining runs (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Sardana et al., 2024). We therefore wonder whether pretraining and supervised finetuning runs are long enough for this relationship to hold; we find it to hold surprisingly precisely in practice, as illustrated in Figure 4. Despite the simplicity and robustness of that result, we are not aware of any prior work that has reported it within the language model literature.

To show this, we run experiments with the OLMo 2 suite of models (Team OLMo, 2025), which provides multiple pretraining and supervised finetuned checkpoints with varying model sizes, as well as the pretraining and finetuning datasets that were used to train the models. For each model size, we evaluate the different checkpoints on both pretraining and finetuning data, and report the entropy as a function of the cross-entropy loss. Overall, the identity holds, both after pretraining and supervised finetuning. Cross-entropy loss decreases as we scale models, so larger models have lower entropy. Figure 9 in the appendix confirms that the same holds for the Pythia suite of models (Biderman et al., 2023). Entropy decreases everywhere during finetuning even though we are using a forward KL objective, which inflates entropy. We reiterate that the inflation is relative to the teacher, and that lower entropy overall reflects the low entropy of the finetuning data, which is for example a well-known property of alignment data (West & Potts, 2025; Lanchantin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Springer et al., 2026).

Zooming out, this result informs us about how pretrained models fail to capture the data distribution: they tend to leak probability mass outside the support of the data distribution rather than overconfidently predicting high probability tokens.

4.2 On-policy distillation’s lower entropy is due to token-level reverse KL

So far, we have focused on the divergence and kept the sampling distribution fixed, which is the setting in which the results of Section 3 hold. On-policy distillation is increasingly used in the posttraining of large language models (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025; Xiao et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026), as training on its own completions removes the exposure bias (Bengio et al., 2015) that models trained off-policy face. It is usually paired with reverse KL, as both follow from the same sequence-level derivation (Gu et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), so that a loss of diversity could a priori come from either choice. In this set of experiments, we ablate the effects of the divergence (forward vs. reverse KL) and the sampling distribution (on-policy vs. off-policy) on entropy. We distill the Qwen3-Instruct models (Yang et al., 2025) in non-thinking mode into a Qwen3-0.6B-Base student on the math problems of DeepScaleR (Luo et al., 2025). We measure entropy on MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024) on student completions in Figure 5, and on frozen teacher completions in Figure 10 in the appendix.

The divergence has the largest effect on entropy: forward KL raises the entropy of the student and reverse KL lowers it, for every teacher and both sampling distributions, consistently with the ordering of Section 3. On-policy distillation consistently yields higher entropy than off-policy distillation, but this effect is two to three times smaller than that of the divergence. Zhao et al. (2026a) similarly report that the prefix source has a much smaller effect on entropy than the direction of the KL, particularly on short completions. On-policy sampling therefore modulates the effect of the divergence, and the lower entropy of on-policy distillation is mainly due to reverse KL. Finally, teacher size barely matters: the three teachers have almost the same entropy on their own completions and are all obtained by distillation from the same larger models (Yang et al., 2025), and Li et al. (2026) have shown that teachers trained with the same pipeline induce nearly identical next-token distributions on the contexts the student visits despite their difference in size.

4.3 Self-distillation deflates entropy, divergence can compensate for it

In self-distillation, the teacher is the student itself, given additional feedback on how to solve the task. This sidesteps the need for a more capable model to distill from, and improves performance on a variety of tasks. Nicolicioiu et al. (2026) have shown that conditioning on task feedback decreases the output diversity of the teacher, and thus that of the student. Here, we focus on how the choice of divergence interacts with this effect. As the teacher is derived from the student, any entropy the student loses is also lost by the teacher, which can lead to entropy collapse.

We follow the experimental setup of Hübotter et al. (2026) on the chemistry subset of SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2024), which consists of multiple-choice questions testing scientific knowledge and reasoning in chemistry. We finetune Olmo 3 7B Instruct (Team Olmo, 2025), starting from the default hyperparameters of Hübotter et al. (2026), and varying three knobs that are important in practice: the divergence within the generalized Jensen–Shannon family, the frequency at which the teacher is updated, and the number of tokens taken into account when computing the divergence. As in the implementation of Hübotter et al. (2026), these tokens are the top-kk tokens of the student. The main results are reported in Figure 6, and we run the same experiments on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) in Appendix C.5, with similar conclusions.

Overall, we find that the default hyperparameters are ones that stabilize entropy, and that moving away from them can lead to entropy collapse. When varying the weight of the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence (Figure 6 left), entropy smoothly decreases with λ\lambda, consistently with the early learning dynamics of the toy model (Figure 2e). In the longer runs of Appendix C.5, entropy sharply increases between λ=0.25\lambda=0.25 and λ=0\lambda=0, although not as abruptly as in the toy model at convergence (Figure 2d). This could be due to the almost on-policy nature of the data, which makes different runs see different contexts. With reverse KL, entropy collapses (Figure 6 left): the entropy deflation of reverse KL compounds with the reduced diversity of the teacher, which in turn lowers the entropy of the next teacher, and so on. Entropy also collapses when the teacher is the live student (Figure 6 center), whereas an exponential moving average, even with a decay of 0.950.95, behaves like a frozen teacher and prevents the collapse. Restricting the divergence to fewer tokens (Figure 6 right) affects entropy as the toy model of Section 3.6 predicts early in training when the student selects the top-kk tokens (Figure 3 left): with the tail bucket, entropy increases as kk decreases, whereas renormalizing leaves it roughly independent of kk. Performance-wise, these different hyperparameters account for differences of a few percentage points as long as entropy does not collapse, cf. Figure 11.

Our results emphasize the importance of separating the choice of divergence from the sampling distribution. Indeed, deriving self-distillation from a sequence-level reverse KL to justify on-policy sampling forces the choice of reverse KL, which collapses entropy and damages performance. This is consistent with self-distillation papers (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b, e.g.,) not finding reverse KL to work best in practice.22 2 Shenfeld et al. (2026) report using reverse KL in the paper, but the code uses forward KL.

5 Conclusion

The divergence used in distillation is often inherited rather than chosen: a sequence-level derivation ties reverse KL to on-policy data and forward KL to off-policy data. Once we disentangled these choices, we found that the divergence, more than the sampling distribution, acts as an implicit regularizer on the student. Forward KL inflates the entropy of the student above that of the teacher by exactly the residual divergence on average, so the entropy of a converged pretraining run can be read from its loss. Reverse KL deflates entropy, but only as long as the student can mimic the teacher; whether it does is a property of the divergence and the task together, not of the divergence alone. In between, and depending on how the tail of the distribution is handled, entropy can be tuned, smoothly early in training and abruptly at convergence. These effects compound in self-distillation, where the teacher is derived from the student: any entropy drop feeds back into the next teacher, and the hyperparameters that work best are those whose inflation counteracts the drop that conditioning on privileged information induces.

Practically, our results suggest choosing the sampling distribution and the divergence separately, and treating the latter as an entropy knob rather than as a consequence of the former.

We obtained these results with a toy model of language modeling, simple enough to admit precise mathematical statements yet rich enough to reproduce key phenomena at scale. We hope that it will replace the Gaussian mixtures inherited from variational inference as the go-to example to reason about distillation in large language models, and that it will prove useful beyond entropy.
