Appendix A The distillation framework

Section 2 introduces the token-level distillation objective of Equation 1 and states that writing the objective at the token level is what decouples the data-generating process pp from the divergence ℓ\ell. This appendix makes that claim precise. We first define the sequence-level objective, the token-level one and the surrogate that implementations actually differentiate, and compare them (Appendix A.1). We then discuss how the token-level objective is evaluated in practice (Appendix A.2) and define the divergence families we sweep over (Appendix A.3).

A.1 Token- and sequence-level objectives and where gradients are stopped

There are a few technical details in how distillation methods are defined, mostly when the completions are sampled from the student, that have important consequences. Here, we emphasize the difference between token- and sequence-level objectives, and review how an implementation detail, the stop-gradient, alters the objective that is actually optimized.

A.1.1 The different objectives
Definition 1 (Sequence-level objective).

The sequence-level objective compares the student and teacher distributions over entire sequences,

ℒseq(θ)=𝔼x[ℓseq(πθ(⋅∣x),π∗(⋅∣x))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\ell_{\mathrm{seq}}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right], (8)

where ℓseq\ell_{\mathrm{seq}} is a divergence between the two probability distributions over the full sequence space. For the reverse KL divergence, ℓseq=DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥π∗(⋅∣x))\ell_{\mathrm{seq}}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\parallel\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)), which hides an expectation over student-generated sequences. The forward KL divergence instead hides an expectation over teacher-generated sequences.

Definition 2 (Token-level objective).

The token-level objective is that of Equation 1,

ℒtok(θ)=𝔼x𝔼y∼p(⋅∣x)[∑t=1Tℓtok(πθ(⋅∣x,y<t),π∗(⋅∣x,y<t))],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{\mathrm{tok}}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right], (9)

with ℓtok\ell_{\mathrm{tok}} a divergence between the token-level distributions in context (x,y<t)(x,y_{<t}) and pp the data-generating process from which the sequences are sampled.

Definition 3 (Surrogate token-level objective).

The surrogate token-level objective ignores the potential dependency of the data-generating process on the parameters:

ℒsur​-​tok(θ)=𝔼x𝔼y∼stop-gradient[p](⋅∣x)[∑t=1Tℓtok(πθ(⋅∣x,y<t),π∗(⋅∣x,y<t))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur\text{-}tok}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\text{stop-gradient}[p](\cdot\mid x)}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{\mathrm{tok}}\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right]. (10)

Its gradient is

∇θℒsur​-​tok=𝔼x𝔼y∼p[∑t∇θℓtok(πθ(⋅∣x,y<t),π∗(⋅∣x,y<t))],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur\text{-}tok}}=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}\left[\sum_{t}\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{\mathrm{tok}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}))\right], (11)

and this is what most papers use in practice.

Remark 1.

When p=π∗p=\pi^{*}, the data-generating process does not depend on θ\theta so the stop-gradient has no effect and ℒsur​-​tok\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur\text{-}tok}} and ℒtok\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}} have the same gradients. The surrogate differs from the token-level objective only when sampling on-policy, i.e. p=πθp=\pi_{\theta}, or more generally when the sampling distribution depends on the student.

A.1.2 How the different objectives and their gradients compare
Fact 1 (The token- and sequence-level objectives can be equal).

Take p=πθp=\pi_{\theta} with ℓtok\ell_{\mathrm{tok}} and ℓseq\ell_{\mathrm{seq}} the reverse KL divergence, or p=π∗p=\pi^{*} with ℓtok\ell_{\mathrm{tok}} and ℓseq\ell_{\mathrm{seq}} the forward KL divergence. Then ℒtok=ℒseq\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}, and in particular ∇θℒtok=∇θℒseq\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{seq}}.

Proof.

The proof relies on the chain rule of the KL divergence, which we state for general autoregressive distributions before applying it to the setting of interest. Let a(⋅∣x)a(\cdot\mid x) and b(⋅∣x)b(\cdot\mid x) be two distributions. Their sequence-level log-ratio decomposes token by token,

log⁡a⁡(y∣x)b⁡(y∣x)=∑t=1Tlog⁡a⁡(yt∣x,y<t)b⁡(yt∣x,y<t).\log\frac{a(y\mid x)}{b(y\mid x)}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{a(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{b(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}. (12)

Taking the expectation under y∼a(⋅∣x)y\sim a(\cdot\mid x) and exchanging it with the finite sum,

DKL(a(⋅∣x)∥b(⋅∣x))=∑t=1T𝔼y∼a(⋅∣x)[loga⁡(yt∣x,y<t)b⁡(yt∣x,y<t)].D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a(\cdot\mid x)\parallel b(\cdot\mid x))=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim a(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\log\frac{a(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{b(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right]. (13)

The tt-th summand depends on yy only through the prefix y<ty_{<t} and the current token yty_{t}, so the future tokens y>ty_{>t} marginalize out (the tower property) and the expectation becomes

𝔼y∼a(⋅∣x)[loga⁡(yt∣x,y<t)b⁡(yt∣x,y<t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{y\sim a(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\log\frac{a(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{b(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right] =𝔼y<t∼a(⋅∣x)𝔼yt∼a(⋅∣x,y<t)[loga⁡(yt∣x,y<t)b⁡(yt∣x,y<t)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim a(\cdot\mid x)}\,\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim a(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})}\left[\log\frac{a(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{b(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right] (14)
=𝔼y<t∼a(⋅∣x)[DKL(a(⋅∣x,y<t)∥b(⋅∣x,y<t))],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y_{<t}\sim a(\cdot\mid x)}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(a(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\parallel b(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right], (15)

the inner expectation being the KL divergence between the token-level distributions in context (x,y<t)(x,y_{<t}). Summing over tt and collecting the per-step expectations back into a single expectation over y∼a(⋅∣x)y\sim a(\cdot\mid x),

DKL(a(⋅∣x)∥b(⋅∣x))=𝔼y∼a(⋅∣x)[∑t=1TDKL(a(⋅∣x,y<t)∥b(⋅∣x,y<t))].D_{\mathrm{KL}}(a(\cdot\mid x)\parallel b(\cdot\mid x))=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim a(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(a(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\parallel b(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right)\right]. (16)

This has exactly the same form as the token-level objective of Definition 2 with the data sampled from aa and ℓtok\ell_{\mathrm{tok}} the per-token KL divergence between aa and bb. The two subcases follow by choosing (a,b)(a,b).

  • –

    Taking a=πθa=\pi_{\theta} and b=π∗b=\pi^{*} gives the reverse KL divergence with p=a=πθp=a=\pi_{\theta}.

  • –

    Taking a=π∗a=\pi^{*} and b=πθb=\pi_{\theta} gives the forward KL divergence with p=a=π∗p=a=\pi^{*}.

In both, the outer expectation samples the prefixes from the first argument of the divergence, which is precisely pp. Equality of the objectives implies equality of their gradients, as there are no stop-gradients or additional implicit parameters held constant here. ∎

Remark 2.

Because the chain rule samples the prefixes from the first argument of the divergence, deriving an objective at the sequence level fixes the data-generating process at the token level: the reverse KL divergence forces p=πθp=\pi_{\theta} and the forward KL divergence forces p=π∗p=\pi^{*}. This is why we argued that sequence-level objectives couple ℓtok\ell_{\mathrm{tok}} to pp in the main text. Conversely, nothing couples the two once the objective is written at the token level from the start, which is what lets us sweep the divergence at a fixed data-generating process in Section 3.

A.1.3 What the stop-gradients used in practice ignore

In practice, the surrogate objective is typically used. It follows that the resulting gradient is a biased estimate of that of the actual objective.

Fact 2 (The token-level gradient and its surrogate).

Write ℓt(y,θ)=ℓtok(πθ(⋅∣x,y<t),π∗(⋅∣x,y<t))\ell_{t}(y,\theta)=\ell_{\mathrm{tok}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})) for the per-token loss along a sequence. The token-level gradient decomposes as

∇θℒtok=∇θℒsur​-​tok+gseq,\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur\text{-}tok}}+g_{\mathrm{seq}}, (17)

with the visitation gradient in its causal form

gseq=𝔼x​𝔼y∼p​[∑s=1T∇θ​log​p​(ys∣x,y<s)​∑t=sTℓt​(y,θ)],g_{\mathrm{seq}}=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}\left[\sum_{s=1}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}\log p(y_{s}\mid x,y_{<s})\sum_{t=s}^{T}\ell_{t}(y,\theta)\right], (18)

each token weighted by its cost-to-go ∑t=sTℓt\sum_{t=s}^{T}\ell_{t}. When p=π∗p=\pi^{*}, gseq=0g_{\mathrm{seq}}=0 and the three gradients coincide. When p=πθp=\pi_{\theta} it is generally nonzero, and only then does the surrogate the algorithm optimizes depart from the true gradient of the objective.

Proof.

Write L⁡(y,θ)=∑tℓt​(y,θ)L(y,\theta)=\sum_{t}\ell_{t}(y,\theta) so that ℒtok=𝔼x​𝔼y∼p​[L]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{tok}}=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}[L], and differentiate the sampled expectation with the score-function identity,

∇θ𝔼y∼p​[L]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}[L] =𝔼y∼p​[∇θL]+𝔼y∼p​[L​∇θ​log⁡p⁡(y∣x)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}\left[\nabla_{\theta}L\right]+\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}\left[L\nabla_{\theta}\log p(y\mid x)\right], (19)

using ∇θp=p​∇θ​log⁡p\nabla_{\theta}p=p\,\nabla_{\theta}\log p. The first term differentiates only the losses, at fixed sampling distribution, and is ∇θℒsur​-​tok\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur\text{-}tok}} of Definition 3; the second is the visitation gradient. When p=π∗p=\pi^{*} does not depend on θ\theta, this score term is absent and gseq=0g_{\mathrm{seq}}=0. It remains to bring the visitation gradient to the causal form of the statement. The score factors over tokens,

∇θ​log​p​(y∣x)=∑s=1T∇θ​log​p​(ys∣x,y<s),\nabla_{\theta}\log p(y\mid x)=\sum_{s=1}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}\log p(y_{s}\mid x,y_{<s}), (20)

and the losses ℓt\ell_{t} with t<st<s do not depend on the token drawn at step ss given its prefix, so, conditioning on y<sy_{<s} and using 𝔼ys∼p(⋅∣x,y<s)[∇θlogp(ys∣x,y<s)]=0\mathbb{E}_{y_{s}\sim p(\cdot\mid x,y_{<s})}[\nabla_{\theta}\log p(y_{s}\mid x,y_{<s})]=0, their cross terms vanish in expectation. Only the cost-to-go ∑t=sTℓt\sum_{t=s}^{T}\ell_{t} survives against the step-ss score, giving the causal form

gseq=𝔼x​𝔼y∼p​[∑s=1T∇θ​log​p​(ys∣x,y<s)​∑t=sTℓt​(y,θ)].g_{\mathrm{seq}}=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p}\left[\sum_{s=1}^{T}\nabla_{\theta}\log p(y_{s}\mid x,y_{<s})\sum_{t=s}^{T}\ell_{t}(y,\theta)\right]. (21)

∎

Remark 3.

The per-token losses ℓt\ell_{t} are per-step costs, and gseqg_{\mathrm{seq}} is the credit assigned to each token for its effect on the future costs it steers the sequence towards. Keeping it in full is the undiscounted, full-horizon policy gradient, which corresponds to a discount factor of γ=1\gamma=1; the surrogate gradient drops it entirely, crediting each token only for its immediate cost, that is the discount factor is taken to be γ=0\gamma=0 (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). The myopic token-level algorithm used in practice is therefore the surrogate, not the sequence-level objective: the two objectives are equal (Fact 1), and it is only the gradient that is truncated. This is why the surrogate dynamics do not in general follow the gradient of any well-defined objective (Czarnecki et al., 2019), the field ∇θℒsur​-​tok\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sur\text{-}tok}} being non-conservative once p=πθp=\pi_{\theta} moves with θ\theta.

Remark 4.

Dropping gseqg_{\mathrm{seq}} is not only a modeling choice and can be a practical necessity. As a score-function estimator over full rollouts, the gradient gseqg_{\mathrm{seq}} is high-variance and expensive to estimate, a difficulty at the heart of reinforcement learning with policy gradients (Williams, 1992; Schulman et al., 2016). It is also the term that makes the student account for how its own choices reshape the sequence distribution on which it is later scored. This is consistent with the reward hacking observed when solely optimizing the sequence-level reverse KL divergence (Gu et al., 2024).

Remark 5.

This is the observation that lets the rest of the paper ignore the sequence-modeling aspects of distillation in our toy model of Section 3.1. Once gseqg_{\mathrm{seq}} is dropped, every gradient the algorithm takes is an average of per-context gradients of ℓtok\ell_{\mathrm{tok}}, and the contexts only enter through the distribution pp that generates them. The toy model of Section 3.1 keeps exactly this structure, a set of contexts and a per-context divergence, and discards the autoregressive coupling between them.

A.2 Practical evaluation of the token-level divergence

Evaluating the token-level divergence ℓ\ell in Equation 1 over the full vocabulary can be expensive. Two strategies reduce this cost: estimating the divergence from a single sampled token, or restricting the sum to a top-kk subset of the vocabulary.

A.2.1 Sampled-token evaluation

Instead of summing over the vocabulary, one can estimate ℓt\ell_{t} from a single sampled token, reducing the cost to a single teacher probability per context. This is the only option when the teacher is implicit, as in next-token cross-entropy during pretraining, but is also used with explicit teachers for efficiency. The gradient of this estimate needs care when the sample comes from the student. We illustrate with the reverse KL, where yt∼πθy_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}; the same applies to the student branch of the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence but not to the forward KL, which samples from the teacher.

Naively differentiating the sampled log-ratio at fixed yty_{t} gives

∇θ​log​πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)π∗​(yt∣x,y<t)=∇θ​log​πθ​(yt∣x,y<t),\nabla_{\theta}\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi^{*}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}), (22)

since the teacher does not depend on θ\theta, and its expected value vanishes as

𝔼yt∼πθ​[∇θ​log​πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)]=0,\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})]=0, (23)

whereas ∇θℓt\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{t} is generally nonzero, because this estimate ignores that the distribution from which yty_{t} is drawn itself depends on θ\theta. Accounting for it through the score-function identity

∇θ𝔼yt∼πθ​[f]=𝔼yt∼πθ​[f​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)+∇θf]\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}[f]=\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}[f\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})+\nabla_{\theta}f] (24)

with ff the log-ratio, the integrand term 𝔼yt∼πθ​[∇θf]\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}[\nabla_{\theta}f] is exactly the vanishing naive estimate above, so only the score-function term remains,

∇θℓt=𝔼yt∼πθ​[log⁡πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)π∗​(yt∣x,y<t)​∇θ​log​πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)].\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{t}=\mathbb{E}_{y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{\pi^{*}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\right]. (25)

This is a second score function, taken at the output token level instead of the sequence level as in the prefix-visitation gradient gseqg_{\mathrm{seq}} of Fact 2.

Practical implementations.

The on-policy distillation recipe of Lu & Thinking Machines Lab (2025) combines this approximation with the one of Remark 3. It estimates ℓt\ell_{t} from the sampled token, using −stop−grad⁡[log⁡(πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)/π∗​(yt∣x,y<t))]-\operatorname{stop-grad}[\log(\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})/\pi^{*}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}))] as a per-token advantage inside a standard policy-gradient pipeline, and it truncates the cost-to-go to the immediate term (γ=0\gamma=0). The first is the Monte Carlo approximation of the local loss gradient over the action space discussed above. The second is the truncation of the sequence-level gradient over time that Appendix A.1 analyzes. The two are independent of each other.

A.2.2 Top-kk restrictions: renormalization and tail bucket

When the teacher’s full probability vector is available, it is common to restrict the divergence to a subset S⊆{1,…,d}S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\} of the vocabulary, typically the top-kk tokens of the teacher or the student, for compute and bandwidth efficiency. Given such a subset, there are two standard ways to handle the probability mass outside SS.

Renormalization.

Both distributions are renormalized over SS and the divergence is computed between the restricted distributions:

ℓrenorm​(πθ,π∗,S)=ℓ⁡(πθ|SMθ,π∗|SM∗),\ell_{\text{renorm}}(\pi_{\theta},\pi^{*};S)=\ell\!\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}|_{S}}{M_{\theta}},\frac{\pi^{*}|_{S}}{M^{*}}\right), (26)

where Mθ=∑j∈Sπθ​(j)M_{\theta}=\sum_{j\in S}\pi_{\theta}(j) and M∗=∑j∈Sπ∗​(j)M^{*}=\sum_{j\in S}\pi^{*}(j) are the total masses on SS, and π|S\pi|_{S} denotes the restriction of π\pi to SS. This discards the tail entirely: the gradient with respect to logits outside SS is zero, and the student receives no signal about how much total mass to place on the top-kk set.

Tail bucket.

All mass outside SS is lumped into a single extra category and the divergence is computed over k+1k+1 tokens:

ℓtail​(πθ,π∗,S)=ℓ⁡(π~θ,π~∗),withπ~​(j)={π⁡(j)j∈S,1−∑j′∈Sπ⁡(j′)j=tail.\ell_{\text{tail}}(\pi_{\theta},\pi^{*};S)=\ell\!\left(\tilde{\pi}_{\theta},\tilde{\pi}^{*}\right),\quad\text{with}\quad\tilde{\pi}(j)=\begin{cases}\pi(j)&j\in S,\\ 1-\sum_{j^{\prime}\in S}\pi(j^{\prime})&j=\text{tail}.\end{cases} (27)

This preserves the total-mass constraint: the student is trained to match the teacher’s tail mass as a lump sum, which provides one additional degree of freedom compared to renormalization.

As Section 3.6 and Appendix B.6 show, the choice between the two has a direct effect on the entropy of the student.

A.3 The divergence families we consider

Forward and reverse KL are the two main focuses of our analysis, but the transition between them is itself informative, so we also train on a family that interpolates between the two. We use the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence, the objective family of Agarwal et al. (2024) also used in other works (Hübotter et al., 2026, e.g.,), which compares both models to their mixture

mλ=λ​π∗+(1−λ)​πθm_{\lambda}=\lambda\pi^{*}+(1-\lambda)\pi_{\theta} (28)

through

JSλ(π∗,πθ)=λDKL(π∗∥mλ)+(1−λ)DKL(πθ∥mλ),\mathrm{JS}_{\lambda}(\pi^{*},\pi_{\theta})=\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel m_{\lambda})+(1-\lambda)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\parallel m_{\lambda}), (29)

with λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1]. The two KL divergences are recovered in the limits, after dividing by the prefactor that vanishes there.

As λ→0\lambda\to 0 the mixture tends to πθ\pi_{\theta}, so

DKL(πθ∥mλ)=O(λ2)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\parallel m_{\lambda})=O(\lambda^{2}) (30)

and

JSλλ→DKL(π∗∥πθ),\frac{\mathrm{JS}_{\lambda}}{\lambda}\to D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta}), (31)

which is the forward KL.

As λ→1\lambda\to 1 the mixture tends to π∗\pi^{*} and symmetrically

JSλ1−λ→DKL(πθ∥π∗),\frac{\mathrm{JS}_{\lambda}}{1-\lambda}\to D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\parallel\pi^{*}), (32)

the reverse KL.

Both endpoints of Equation 29 are identically zero, so only the interior of the family has a gradient; we take the divergence at λ=0\lambda=0 and λ=1\lambda=1 to be its normalized limits, that is the exact forward and reverse KL, which makes the whole interval trainable, matching the implementations of Agarwal et al. (2024) and von Werra et al. (2020). This scale mismatch is not a problem to compare learning dynamics and their observables (like entropy), as Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) is almost invariant to the overall scale of the loss (Balles & Hennig, 2018).

ff-divergences.

Throughout the theory, we will sometimes use results that hold for a broad class of divergences, ff-divergences, which includes the generalized Jensen–Shannon family and its two endpoints. We introduce them here for completeness and make the connection to the generalized Jensen–Shannon family explicit. Given a convex function ff with f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0, the ff-divergence of a distribution aa from a reference distribution bb is

Df(a∥b)=∑jb(j)f(a⁡(j)b⁡(j)).D_{f}(a\parallel b)=\sum_{j}b(j)f\left(\frac{a(j)}{b(j)}\right). (33)

The reverse KL is recovered with f⁡(t)=t​log⁡tf(t)=t\log t, the forward KL with f⁡(t)=−log⁡tf(t)=-\log t, and the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence with

fλ​(t)=−λ​log⁡(λ+(1−λ)​t)+(1−λ)​t​log⁡tλ+(1−λ)​t.f_{\lambda}(t)=-\lambda\log\big(\lambda+(1-\lambda)t\big)+(1-\lambda)t\log\frac{t}{\lambda+(1-\lambda)t}. (34)

What will matter to us is that all members of this class that are twice differentiable at 11 share the same local geometry around a=ba=b, namely the Fisher metric scaled by the curvature f′′​(1)f^{\prime\prime}(1), which is the statement of Appendix B.1 and what makes the diffuse limit of Appendix B.5 divergence-independent. That curvature is f′′​(1)=1f^{\prime\prime}(1)=1 for both KL directions and fλ′′​(1)=λ⁡(1−λ)f_{\lambda}^{\prime\prime}(1)=\lambda(1-\lambda) for the generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence, which vanishes at the two endpoints and is brought back to 11 by the 1/λ1/\lambda and 1/(1−λ)1/(1-\lambda) normalizations above.

Appendix B Theory

B.1 Divergence choice does not matter around optimality

We now show the claim of Section 3.2: at a fixed data-generating process, the forward and reverse KL objectives have the same gradient to first order around πθ=π∗\pi_{\theta}=\pi^{*}. The statement is per context, so fix a context ii and write πθ\pi_{\theta} and π∗\pi^{*} for the two next-token distributions there. The forward KL gradient is

∇θDKL(π∗∥πθ)=−∑jπ∗(j)∇θlogπθ(j),\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta})=-\sum_{j}\pi^{*}(j)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(j), (35)

the teacher being independent of θ\theta. For the reverse KL, differentiating the product and using ∇θπθ=πθ​∇θ​log⁡πθ\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}=\pi_{\theta}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta} gives

∇θDKL(πθ∥π∗)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\parallel\pi^{*}) =∑j∇θπθ​(j)​log⁡(πθ​(j)π∗​(j))+∑jπθ​(j)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(j)\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(j)\log\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(j)}{\pi^{*}(j)}\right)+\sum_{j}\pi_{\theta}(j)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(j) (36)
=∑jπθ​(j)​∇θ​log⁡πθ​(j)​log⁡(πθ​(j)π∗​(j)),\displaystyle=\sum_{j}\pi_{\theta}(j)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(j)\log\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(j)}{\pi^{*}(j)}\right), (37)

the second term vanishing by the vocabulary-level score identity of Equation 23. Around optimality the log ratio linearizes as

log⁡(πθ​(j)π∗​(j))=−log⁡(π∗​(j)πθ​(j))≈1−π∗​(j)πθ​(j),\log\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(j)}{\pi^{*}(j)}\right)=-\log\left(\frac{\pi^{*}(j)}{\pi_{\theta}(j)}\right)\approx 1-\frac{\pi^{*}(j)}{\pi_{\theta}(j)}, (38)

and substituting it, the constant term vanishes by the score identity again, leaving

∇θDKL(πθ∥π∗)≈−∑jπ∗(j)∇θlogπθ(j)=∇θDKL(π∗∥πθ).\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\parallel\pi^{*})\approx-\sum_{j}\pi^{*}(j)\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(j)=\nabla_{\theta}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta}). (39)

Averaging the two sides over contexts sampled from any data-generating process pp preserves the equality, as pp only weights the contexts and weights them identically on both sides. This is why the statement is independent of pp: the surrogate gradients of Definition 3 for the forward and the reverse KL agree to first order whatever the data-generating process is, as long as it is held fixed. Near optimality, the choice between the two divergences is therefore immaterial, and whatever difference remains between two distillation runs has to come from the data they are trained on.

This equivalence is well known: it is a classical result from information geometry that all suitably standardized ff-divergences, of which forward and reverse KL are special cases, agree up to second order around πθ=π∗\pi_{\theta}=\pi^{*}, with the shared local quadratic form given by the Fisher information metric (Amari, 2016; Polyanskiy & Wu, 2025). The whole generalized Jensen–Shannon family of Appendix A.3 is therefore also equivalent to its two endpoints in this regime.

Importantly, the expansion above requires the perturbation πθ−π∗\pi_{\theta}-\pi^{*} to be small relative to π∗\pi^{*} on every token, that is |log⁡(πθ​(j)/π∗​(j))||\log(\pi_{\theta}(j)/\pi^{*}(j))| uniformly small. This is a much stronger requirement than a small average KL divergence, since the KL weights log ratios by probability mass and is therefore blind to large relative perturbations on low-probability tokens, which is precisely where the gradients of the two objectives differ.

B.2 Where the entropy gap changes sign

Figure 2 varies the number of contexts, the teacher perplexity and the interpolation weight one at a time. Figure 7 repeats this experiment in the plane of number of contexts and teacher perplexity, over 55 different generalized Jensen–Shannon divergence weights λ\lambda. The results highlight that even though sweeping individual parameters yields sharp phase transitions, the boundary of the phase transition evolves much more smoothly.

B.3 The forward KL inflates entropy

This appendix gives the formal backing for the claim in Section 3.3 that the forward KL inflates entropy. Assume the student family is closed under temperature scaling of the logits, which holds for any softmax model whose final linear layer can be rescaled, including standard language model heads. As above we write ii for a context, πθfor∗(⋅∣i)\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}(\cdot\mid i) for the student at a stationary point θfor∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}} of the forward KL objective and z⁡(i)z(i) for its logits there, and take the contexts to be drawn from a data-generating process pp that is held fixed, as the surrogate objective of Definition 3 does.

Define g⁡(i)=𝔼πθfor∗​[z⁡(i)]−𝔼π∗​[z⁡(i)]g(i)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}}[z(i)]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}[z(i)], the mean-logit mismatch in context ii, which is also the derivative of the loss in ii when sharpening the logits along the temperature direction. To see this, perturb the logits along the temperature direction, z⁡(i,ε)=(1+ε)​z​(i)z(i,\varepsilon)=(1+\varepsilon)z(i), so that the loss in ii becomes

ℓfor​(i,ε)=−(1+ε)​𝔼π∗​[z⁡(i)]+log⁡Z⁡(i,ε)\ell^{\mathrm{for}}(i,\varepsilon)=-(1+\varepsilon)\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}[z(i)]+\log Z(i,\varepsilon) (40)

up to a term that does not depend on the student, with Z⁡(i,ε)=∑jexp⁡(z​(i,ε)j)Z(i,\varepsilon)=\sum_{j}\exp(z(i,\varepsilon)_{j}) the partition function of the perturbed student. Using ∇z​log​Z=πθfor∗(ε)\nabla_{z}\log Z=\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}^{(\varepsilon)}, the chain rule gives

dd​ε​ℓfor​(i,ε)=−𝔼π∗​[z⁡(i)]+𝔼πθfor∗(ε)​[z⁡(i)],\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\ell^{\mathrm{for}}(i,\varepsilon)=-\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}[z(i)]+\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}^{(\varepsilon)}}[z(i)], (41)

which at ε=0\varepsilon=0 reduces to

dd​ε​ℓfor​(i,0)=𝔼πθfor∗​[z⁡(i)]−𝔼π∗​[z⁡(i)]=g⁡(i).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\ell^{\mathrm{for}}(i,0)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}}[z(i)]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}[z(i)]=g(i). (42)

At any interior stationary point of the objective, the derivative of the total loss along the temperature direction must vanish, which is exactly

𝔼i​[g​(i)]=0,\mathbb{E}_{i}[g(i)]=0, (43)

the expectation being over contexts drawn from pp, each token counting once as in Equation 1.

The difference in entropy between the student and the teacher can be rewritten to make its dependence on gg explicit:

H⁡(πθfor∗)−H⁡(π∗)\displaystyle H(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})-H(\pi^{*}) =−𝔼πθfor∗​[log⁡πθfor∗]+𝔼π∗​[log⁡π∗]\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}\left[\log\pi^{*}\right] (44)
=𝔼π∗​[log⁡π∗−log⁡πθfor∗]+𝔼π∗​[log⁡πθfor∗]−𝔼πθfor∗​[log⁡πθfor∗]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}\left[\log\pi^{*}-\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}\right] (45)
=DKL(π∗∥πθfor∗)+𝔼π∗[z(i)−logZ(i)]−𝔼πθfor∗[z(i)−logZ(i)]\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})+\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}\left[z(i)-\log Z(i)\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}}\left[z(i)-\log Z(i)\right] (46)
=DKL(π∗∥πθfor∗)−g(i),\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})-g(i), (47)

where the last equality comes from the fact that log⁡Z\log Z is constant in the token and therefore cancels. Leveraging the stationarity condition on gg (Equation 43) yields

𝔼i[H(πθfor∗)]=𝔼i[H(π∗)]+𝔼i[DKL(π∗∥πθfor∗)].\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[H(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})\right]=\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[H(\pi^{*})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})\right]. (48)

Note that nothing in the argument constrains pp: the identity is a property of the forward KL alone, the data-generating process only setting which contexts the two averages run over. When the teacher is implicit and only accessible through its samples, as in pretraining, the right-hand side is the cross-entropy loss, which gives the form of Equation 6 that Section 4.1 tests.

This is an instance of a classical fact from information geometry: along its temperature direction, the student is a one-parameter exponential family with its own logits as sufficient statistic. Stationarity of the forward KL divergence is moment matching of that statistic (Wainwright & Jordan, 2008), and the entropy of a moment-matched projection exceeds the entropy of its target by exactly their divergence (Amari, 2016).

From average to pointwise inflation.

So far, we have shown that entropy increases when averaging over contexts. A natural follow-up question is whether the same holds in each context individually, that is, whether the entropy gap is always positive, or equivalently whether g(i)<DKL(π∗∥πθfor∗)g(i)<D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}) everywhere. The statement becomes pointwise as soon as the family contains per-context temperature directions, meaning that for every context the perturbation rescaling z⁡(i)z(i) while leaving the logits in other contexts unchanged is tangent to the family. This is the case when the model has a learned input-dependent temperature on its logits, and approximately when the body is expressive enough to rescale its last-layer representation in one context without affecting the others. Stationarity along these directions forces g⁡(i)=0g(i)=0 separately in every context, and the identity becomes

H(πθfor∗)=H(π∗)+DKL(π∗∥πθfor∗)H(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}})=H(\pi^{*})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^{*}\parallel\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{for}}}) (49)

in every context: the student entropy is strictly inflated wherever the student fails to match the teacher, by exactly the misfit there. Note that per-context temperature scaling is far weaker than realizability, as a single scalar per context cannot match a full distribution, so the pointwise statement is not vacuous. This average-versus-pointwise structure echoes the calibration literature, where stationarity along a single shared rescaling direction yields guarantees that hold on average over inputs (Clarté et al., 2023), while near-optimality against richer families of input-dependent post-processings yields correspondingly stronger pointwise ones (Błasiok et al., 2023).

B.4 Reverse KL: a flatness statement

A general statement on entropy similar to the one we obtained for the forward KL does not hold for the reverse one. We apply the same recipe, decomposing the misfit and then exploiting stationarity along the temperature direction, but it yields only a flatness statement. Writing πθrev∗\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}} for the student at a stationary point θrev∗\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}} of the reverse KL objective and expanding the divergence as

DKL(πθrev∗∥π∗)=𝔼πθrev∗[logπθrev∗]−𝔼πθrev∗[logπ∗]=𝔼πθrev∗[−logπ∗]−H(πθrev∗),D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}\parallel\pi^{*})=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}[\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}[\log\pi^{*}]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}[-\log\pi^{*}]-H(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}), (50)

adding H⁡(πθrev∗)H(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}) and subtracting H⁡(π∗)H(\pi^{*}) and rearranging gives, in every context,

H(πθrev∗)=H(π∗)+Δ(i)−DKL(πθrev∗∥π∗)withΔ(i)=𝔼πθrev∗[−logπ∗]−H(π∗).H(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}})=H(\pi^{*})+\Delta(i)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}\parallel\pi^{*})\quad\text{with}\quad\Delta(i)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}[-\log\pi^{*}]-H(\pi^{*}). (51)

The excess surprisal Δ⁡(i)\Delta(i) measures how much more surprising the student’s samples are to the teacher than the teacher’s own samples are.

The student is therefore less confident than the teacher exactly when Δ⁡(i)\Delta(i) exceeds the misfit DKL(πθrev∗∥π∗)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}\parallel\pi^{*}). The temperature-direction argument no longer pins this sign down; it instead yields a flatness statement. Perturbing the logits along the temperature direction, the derivative of the reverse KL loss in context ii is

dd​ε​ℓrev​(i,0)=Varπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗)−Covπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗,log⁡π∗).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\varepsilon}\ell^{\mathrm{rev}}(i,0)=\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}})-\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}},\log\pi^{*}). (52)

Requiring the total derivative to vanish gives the stationarity condition on average over contexts,

𝔼i​[Varπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗)]=𝔼i​[Covπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗,log⁡π∗)].\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}})\right]=\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}},\log\pi^{*})\right]. (53)

Bounding each covariance by Cauchy–Schwarz,

Covπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗,log⁡π∗)≤Varπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗)​Varπθrev∗​(log⁡π∗),\mathrm{Cov}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}},\log\pi^{*})\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}})\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi^{*})}, (54)

applying Cauchy–Schwarz a second time to the average over contexts, dividing by 𝔼i​[Varπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗)]\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{i}[\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}})]} and squaring gives

𝔼i​[Varπθrev∗​(log⁡πθrev∗)]≤𝔼i​[Varπθrev∗​(log⁡π∗)].\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}})\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[\mathrm{Var}_{\pi_{\theta^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}}}(\log\pi^{*})\right]. (55)

As a result, the same techniques that provided an entropy statement for the forward KL only provide a flatness statement here.

B.5 Reverse KL inflates entropy in the diffuse high-load limit

Empirically (Figure 2), we find that when the number of contexts is large (high load) or the teacher is diffuse (high perplexity), the reverse KL stops being mode-seeking and inflates entropy, as the forward KL does. Here, we expand the distillation objective around a diffuse teacher and show that to leading order, forward KL, reverse KL and the whole generalized Jensen–Shannon family reduce to the same quadratic objective and therefore share the same solution. This is why the top right corner of Figure 7 in which both the teacher perplexity and the number of contexts are largest looks the same for every divergence.

The setup.

We work in the toy model of Section 3.1, in which the teacher π∗(⋅∣i)\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i) is drawn independently of the embedding eie_{i}, from a law that is invariant under permutations of the vocabulary. Stack the embeddings into E∈ℝn×hE\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times h}, whose ii-th row is ei⊤e_{i}^{\top}, and write PEP_{E} for the orthogonal projector onto its column space in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. For simplicity, we assume that n>hn>h. Random embeddings are in general position, so rank⁡(E)=h\mathrm{rank}(E)=h. The student head produces the logit matrix Zθ=E​W⊤∈ℝn×dZ_{\theta}=EW^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, so each of its columns is constrained to the hh-dimensional column space of EE. The ratio h/nh/n is therefore the fraction of the nn context directions the student can exactly represent.

The diffuse limit.

We make the teacher diffuse, keeping h/nh/n arbitrary. We model it by fixing the teacher logits z∗​(i)z^{*}(i) and scaling them down by a factor β→0\beta\to 0, so that the teacher distribution becomes uniform in the limit. Write the teacher and the student in centered logit coordinates,

π∗(⋅∣i)\displaystyle\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i) =softmax⁡(β​z∗​(i)),\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}\big(\beta z^{*}(i)\big), (56)
πθ(⋅∣i)\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i) =softmax​(zθ​(i)),\displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}\big(z_{\theta}(i)\big), (57)
𝟏⊤​z∗​(i)\displaystyle\mathbf{1}^{\top}z^{*}(i) =𝟏⊤​zθ​(i)=0,\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}^{\top}z_{\theta}(i)=0, (58)

with the logits z∗​(i)z^{*}(i) fixed and drawn independently across contexts.

All ff-divergences that are twice differentiable at 11 agree to second order around coinciding distributions, and their common quadratic form is the Fisher metric scaled by f′′​(1)f^{\prime\prime}(1) (Amari, 2016); this is the argument we used in Appendix B.1 for the two KL directions. In logit coordinates it reads

Df(softmax(z+δ)∥softmax(z))=f′′​(1)2Varsoftmax⁡(z)(δ)+O(∥δ∥3),D_{f}\big(\mathrm{softmax}(z+\delta)\parallel\mathrm{softmax}(z)\big)=\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(1)}{2}\mathrm{Var}_{\mathrm{softmax}(z)}(\delta)+O(\lVert\delta\rVert^{3}), (59)

the variance being over tokens drawn from the reference distribution, the second argument of DfD_{f}. The expansion holds as long as the offset δ\delta is small, which here means that all the logits involved are O⁡(β)O(\beta): the teacher’s by construction, and the student’s because we expand around the branch on which it stays that close to uniform. We apply it with the teacher as the reference and δ=zθ​(i)−β​z∗​(i)\delta=z_{\theta}(i)-\beta z^{*}(i). The teacher is itself O⁡(β)O(\beta) away from the uniform distribution, so Varπ∗\mathrm{Var}_{\pi^{*}} can in turn be replaced by Varu\mathrm{Var}_{u} at the price of a further O⁡(β3)O(\beta^{3}) term, and for centered logits Varu​(δ)=∥δ∥2/d\mathrm{Var}_{u}(\delta)=\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}/d. Stacking the logits into Z∗,Zθ∈ℝn×dZ^{*},Z_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, this gives

𝔼i[Df(πθ(⋅∣i)∥π∗(⋅∣i))]=f′′​(1)2​n​d∥Zθ−βZ∗∥F2+O(β3).\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[D_{f}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i)\big)\right]=\frac{f^{\prime\prime}(1)}{2nd}\lVert Z_{\theta}-\beta Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}+O(\beta^{3}). (60)

Both KL directions are of this form, with π∗\pi^{*} as the reference distribution and f′′​(1)=1f^{\prime\prime}(1)=1, so they have the same minimizer. The same argument applies to the generalized Jensen–Shannon family of Appendix A.3.

Minimizing Equation 60 over the achievable logits Zθ=E​W⊤Z_{\theta}=EW^{\top} is a least-squares projection onto the column space of EE, so the optimal student logits are

Zθ⋆=β​PE​Z∗+O⁡(β2).Z_{\theta}^{\star}=\beta P_{E}Z^{*}+O(\beta^{2}). (61)

The teacher’s logits have scale O⁡(β)O(\beta), the fitted ones only O⁡(β​h/n)O(\beta\sqrt{h/n}): the entries of Z∗Z^{*} are independent and PEP_{E} is a projector of rank hh that does not depend on them, so

𝔼Z∗​∥PE​Z∗∥F2=hn​𝔼Z∗​∥Z∗∥F2.\mathbb{E}_{Z^{*}}\lVert P_{E}Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}=\frac{h}{n}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{*}}\lVert Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}. (62)

As a result, increasing the number of contexts while keeping the model size fixed, which is what we do in our experiments, makes the student logits smaller relative to the teacher’s, and the student distribution closer to uniform.

Entropy inflation.

Applying Equation 59 again, this time with the uniform distribution as the reference and combining it with DKL(π∥u)=logd−H(π)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\parallel u)=\log d-H(\pi) provides an entropy expansion: a distribution softmax⁡(δ)\mathrm{softmax}(\delta) with small centered logits has entropy

H⁡(softmax⁡(δ))=log⁡d−∥δ∥2/(2​d)+O⁡(∥δ∥3).H(\mathrm{softmax}(\delta))=\log d-\lVert\delta\rVert^{2}/(2d)+O(\lVert\delta\rVert^{3}). (63)

Applying this to the teacher and to the student at the optimum of Equation 61,

H¯​(π∗)=log⁡d−β22​n​d​∥Z∗∥F2+O⁡(β3),H¯​(πθ)=log⁡d−β22​n​d​∥PE​Z∗∥F2+O⁡(β3),\bar{H}(\pi^{*})=\log d-\frac{\beta^{2}}{2nd}\lVert Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}+O(\beta^{3}),\qquad\bar{H}(\pi_{\theta})=\log d-\frac{\beta^{2}}{2nd}\lVert P_{E}Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}+O(\beta^{3}), (64)

so that

H¯​(πθ)−H¯​(π∗)=β22​n​d​∥(I−PE)​Z∗∥F2+O⁡(β3).\bar{H}(\pi_{\theta})-\bar{H}(\pi^{*})=\frac{\beta^{2}}{2nd}\lVert(I-P_{E})Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}+O(\beta^{3}). (65)

That is, for small enough β\beta values, the student inflates entropy relative to the teacher.

If we further assume that the numbers of contexts and tokens are large enough that we can replace the teacher-related quantities by their expected values, the entropy gap only depends on the student through the single ratio h/nh/n. Indeed

𝔼Z∗​∥(I−PE)​Z∗∥F2=(1−hn)​𝔼Z∗​∥Z∗∥F2,\mathbb{E}_{Z^{*}}\lVert(I-P_{E})Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}=\left(1-\frac{h}{n}\right)\mathbb{E}_{Z^{*}}\lVert Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}, (66)

so that Equation 65 becomes

H¯​(πθ)−H¯​(π∗)\displaystyle\bar{H}(\pi_{\theta})-\bar{H}(\pi^{*}) =β22​n​d​(1−hn)​𝔼Z∗​∥Z∗∥F2+O⁡(β3)\displaystyle=\frac{\beta^{2}}{2nd}\left(1-\frac{h}{n}\right)\mathbb{E}_{Z^{*}}\lVert Z^{*}\rVert_{F}^{2}+O(\beta^{3})
=(1−hn)​(log⁡d−H¯​(π∗))+O⁡(β3),\displaystyle=\left(1-\frac{h}{n}\right)\left(\log d-\bar{H}(\pi^{*})\right)+O(\beta^{3}), (67)

the second line recognizing in the first the teacher’s entropy deficit below uniform of Equation 64. It follows that, in the diffuse high-load limit, the gap increases as the number of contexts nn increases, and decreases as the perplexity of the teacher increases, consistently with Figure 2b and 2c.

Evaluating Equation 60 at the optimum and comparing it to Equation 65 gives one last identity,

𝔼i[Df(πθ(⋅∣i)∥π∗(⋅∣i))]=f′′(1)(H¯(πθ)−H¯(π∗))+O(β3),\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[D_{f}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)\parallel\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i)\big)\right]=f^{\prime\prime}(1)\left(\bar{H}(\pi_{\theta})-\bar{H}(\pi^{*})\right)+O(\beta^{3}), (68)

so for either KL direction the residual divergence equals the entropy inflation. For the forward KL this is Equation 6, which holds for any number of contexts and any teacher; reverse KL obeys it too in the diffuse limit.

B.6 Additional results on top-kk

Figure 3 studies the effect of the different top-kk approximations for the forward KL only. The forward KL is the λ=0\lambda=0 endpoint of the generalized Jensen–Shannon family. Figure 8 repeats the experiment at five different generalized Jensen–Shannon weights of Figure 7. The vocabulary size is 6464, so k=64k=64 is the untruncated objective we use in the rest of the toy model experiments. Renormalizing a top-11 distribution gives a Dirac on one token for both student and teacher, so the divergence is identically zero and no learning occurs; we therefore remove this configuration from all our experiments.

B.7 Setup of the toy model experiments

This section details the toy model of Section 3.1 and the simulations of Figures 2, 3, 7 and 8.

Model.

The vocabulary has d=64d=64 tokens and the embeddings have dimension h=128h=128. Each of the nn contexts is assigned an embedding eie_{i} drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution in ℝh\mathbb{R}^{h} and normalized to unit norm, which stays fixed during training. The student is a linear layer followed by a softmax, πθ(⋅∣i)=softmax(Wei+b)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid i)=\mathrm{softmax}(We_{i}+b), with W∈ℝd×hW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times h} initialized with LeCun normal initialization and bb initialized at zero. The main text omits the bias bb for simplicity.

Teachers.

For each context ii, we draw a target perplexity PiP_{i} and Gaussian logits ζi∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\zeta_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), and set π∗(⋅∣i)=softmax(ζi/τi)\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i)=\mathrm{softmax}(\zeta_{i}/\tau_{i}), with the temperature τi\tau_{i} chosen so that H(π∗(⋅∣i))=logPiH(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid i))=\log P_{i}. By default, the perplexities are drawn independently and log-uniformly in [1,16][1,16], so that contexts differ both in which tokens the teacher favors and in how diffuse it is. The teacher perplexity sweep of Figure 2c and the heatmaps of Figure 7 instead give the same perplexity to all contexts. All contexts have the same weight in the objective.

Training.

Every step uses all contexts, and the student is trained with Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015) and a constant learning rate of 0.10.1 for 40,00040{,}000 steps. All results are averaged over 55 seeds, each of which redraws the embeddings, the teachers and the initialization.

Sweeps.

The default number of contexts is n=2048n=2048. Figure 2b uses 2121 values of nn log-spaced between 192192 and 67,58467{,}584, Figure 2c uses 2121 perplexities log-spaced between 11 and 3232, and Figure 2d uses 2121 weights λ\lambda log-spaced between 0.0010.001 and 0.990.99. The trajectories of Figure 2e and the heatmaps of Figure 7 use λ∈{0,0.01,0.1,0.5,1}\lambda\in\{0,0.01,0.1,0.5,1\}, the heatmaps over 1010 perplexities log-spaced between 1.51.5 and 3232 and 88 numbers of contexts log-spaced between 128128 and 40964096. The top-kk experiments of Figures 3 and 8 use n=512n=512 contexts and k∈{1,4,16,64}k\in\{1,4,16,64\}, and Figure 8 uses the same five weights λ\lambda as Figure 7.

Appendix C Additional experimental results

C.1 The identity across model families and pretraining stages

Figure 4 only covers one family of models, OLMo 2 (Team OLMo, 2025), and only at the end of its pretraining. Figure 9 extends it to the Pythia family of models (Biderman et al., 2023) and to an earlier point of OLMo 2’s pretraining, averaging entropy and cross-entropy over about two million tokens per checkpoint.

OLMo 2 is pretrained in two stages, a long first one on a large web-dominated mixture and a short second one on a smaller and higher quality mixture, over which the learning rate is annealed to zero. The light points are the checkpoints at the end of the first stage, measured on the first-stage mixture, and the dark ones the final pretrained models, measured on the second-stage mixture, which is the configuration Figure 4 reports. The pretraining mixture of Figure 4 is therefore the second-stage mixture, the last data the pretrained models were trained on. We draw the same number of tokens from every source of the mixture, but average entropy and cross-entropy at the published proportions of that mixture.

We use the standard Pythia models rather than their deduplicated variants. They are trained in a single stage on the Pile (Gao et al., 2020), whose training stream is released pre-tokenized and in the order the models consumed it, so the tokens we measure on are exactly the ones the models were trained on. Since that run is a single epoch, position in the stream is position in training time, and we sample three chunks of equal size from its beginning, middle and near its end.

C.2 Additional on- vs. off-policy distillation results

Figure 5 only reports the entropy of the student on its own completions. Figure 10 completes it with the entropy of the student on frozen teacher completions, where the contexts cannot move and only the weights can, and with its accuracy. Accuracy is the in-training evaluation, averaged over one sample on 200200 MATH500 problems at the evaluation budget of Table 1, and is therefore noisier than the endpoint evaluation.

On frozen teacher completions, forward KL inflates entropy and reverse KL deflates it, and off-policy reverse KL deflates it most. On the student’s own completions the split has the same sign, with on-policy forward KL inflating entropy most. Reverse KL slightly improves accuracy over the base student while forward KL, in particular on-policy, degrades it.

The lower accuracy of forward KL may largely be a consequence of the different levels of entropy it reaches rather than of what the student learns. The in-training evaluation samples at temperature 11, and a student with more entropy is more likely to sample a wrong token along a long solution. Consistently, at the lower sampling temperature of the endpoint evaluation (Appendix C.3), all twelve runs score above the base student on MATH500, between 43.00%43.00\% and 46.27%46.27\% against 42.87%42.87\%. We expect accuracy to vary smoothly with entropy in this regime, so that the sampling temperature, or the other hyperparameters, could likely be adjusted to recover part of this gap. We did not try to: we kept the hyperparameters of Zhao et al. (2026a) fixed across the grid and did not tune them for accuracy, as our goal is to study entropy. These results should therefore only be read as showing that some of these settings improve the accuracy of the student, not as a comparison of the best accuracy each objective can reach.

C.3 Setup of the on- vs. off-policy distillation experiments

These experiments vary the sampling distribution and the divergence independently, as in Section 2, on a standard reasoning distillation task. Following Zhao et al. (2026a), we distill the Qwen3 instruct models with thinking disabled, at 1.71.7B, 44B and 88B parameters, into Qwen3-0.6B-Base (Yang et al., 2025), on the math problems of DeepScaleR (Luo et al., 2025). The prefixes on which the token-level divergence is evaluated are either completions sampled from the teacher once and cached before training (off-policy), or completions sampled from the current student at every step (on-policy). The divergence is either the forward or the reverse KL, computed on the full vocabulary at every position of the prefix. Crossing the two prefix sources with the two divergences gives four objectives, and with three teachers the grid consists of twelve runs, all starting from the same base student. Table 1 lists the hyperparameters, which follow Zhao et al. (2026a) except for the choices motivated below.

The prompt frame.

A token-level divergence compares the two models on the same prefix, so they have to share a prompt frame, yet they work best in different ones. The base student degrades inside the chat template, from 42.87%42.87\% to 14.93%14.93\% accuracy on MATH500 (Lightman et al., 2024), whereas the instruct teachers remain accurate outside of it but almost never stop, as there is no turn to end. We therefore prompt both models without chat template, with the problem text followed by the instruction “Let’s think step by step and output the final answer within \boxed{}.”, cut each teacher completion right after its first boxed answer, and append the end-of-text token of the student. This avoids a format warmup stage, which would amount to off-policy forward KL distillation, that is, to one of the four objectives being compared.

The teacher corpus and the training length.

Teacher completions are sampled at temperature 11 without top-pp or top-kk truncation, unlike in Zhao et al. (2026a), because the objective is an expectation under the distribution of the teacher. Completions without a boxed answer within 40964096 tokens are dropped, which keeps about two thirds of them and biases the corpus towards problems that the teacher solves concisely. Training runs for 800800 steps of 3232 prompts, just below one pass over the smallest corpus, so that no teacher benefits from more repetitions than another. We add Qwen3-1.7B to the two teachers of Zhao et al. (2026a) because Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B are statistically indistinguishable on AMC23 (66.2%66.2\% against 66.6%66.6\% accuracy).

Evaluation.

We measure the entropy of the student on its own completions, whose contexts drift during training, and on a fixed set of cached teacher completions, on which only the weights of the student can change. Evaluation completions are generated with a fixed seed, so that neighboring evaluation points share contexts. We report the entropy pooled across tokens, as Zhao et al. (2026a) do. As it weights each completion by its length, on the student’s own completions it also moves when which completions are long changes, and the per-sequence average, which we also log, can disagree with it in sign. The frozen MATH500 completions keep all 200200 problems, whereas the held-out DeepScaleR problems go through the same filtering as the training corpus and differ from one teacher to the other, so we compare teachers on MATH500 only. Endpoint accuracy is measured at temperature 0.60.6 and top-pp 0.950.95 with a budget of 81928192 tokens, averaged over three samples per problem.

Pure bfloat16 training freezes the normalization gains.

Following Zhao et al. (2026a), we train in bfloat16 without float32 master weights. All normalization gains then stay bit-identical throughout training, as the bfloat16 spacing at their typical magnitude is four orders of magnitude above the optimizer step, while the weight matrices do move. As the final normalization gain controls the scale of the logits, these runs cannot test any statement about that scale, and we make none.

C.4 Accuracy vs. entropy for self-distillation on the Chemistry dataset

Figure 6 only reported the entropy of the student over time on the Chemistry dataset. We report the corresponding accuracy in Figure 11 for the sake of completeness.

C.5 Additional self-distillation experiments on GSM8K

The main text follows the experimental setup of Hübotter et al. (2026) on the Chemistry dataset. We repeat it here on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) with Qwen3-0.6B (Yang et al., 2025), a testbed cheap enough to sweep the learning rate and to train ten times longer; Table 2 lists the hyperparameters of both setups. Figure 12 is the counterpart of Figure 6, at a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, and shows the same qualitative behavior: entropy decreases monotonically with the generalized Jensen–Shannon weight λ\lambda, a teacher that follows the student too closely collapses, and restricting the divergence to fewer tokens raises entropy.

The learning rate sweep of Figure 13 shows that the more a configuration deflates entropy, the smaller the learning rate it tolerates. Reverse KL already loses to the base model at 10−510^{-5}, whereas the arms closer to forward KL keep improving up to 3⋅10−53\cdot 10^{-5}, and a slowly moving or frozen teacher tolerates rates at which a live one has already collapsed.

We finally use the same testbed to train ten times longer, and ask whether the sharp dependence of entropy on λ\lambda that the toy model predicts at convergence (Figure 2d) appears once the runs are long enough. Figure 14 shows that entropy does settle within 500500 steps. The trajectories separate the two behaviors of Section 3 cleanly: the forward KL arm has entropy much larger than its initial value, while every arm with λ>0\lambda>0 settles below it. The ordering in λ\lambda holds at every point of the trajectory, and it leaves the gap between λ=0\lambda=0 and λ=0.25\lambda=0.25 as by far the largest of the sweep, as a phase transition inside that interval would predict. Five weights spaced 0.250.25 apart are too coarse to confirm it. However, note that each run is evaluated on on-policy data, that is run-specific data, whereas the data was exactly the same in the toy setup.
